claims.text: E2B supports memory plus filesystem snapshots and fork() of up to 20 copies per call in its SDKs; its egress is open by default, with allow/deny rules by domain, CIDR, or IP (allow wins), runtime updates, and header injection (beta).

E2B pause saves both filesystem and memory, so running processes and loaded variables survive; pausing takes about 4 seconds per GiB of RAM, resuming about 1 second, and a paused sandbox is kept indefinitely until killed.
E2B checkpoint/restore can snapshot the entire disk state in about 300 milliseconds, while sandbox creation takes 1 to 12 seconds.
Firecracker cold boot takes 125-200ms; with snapshot-restore it drops to 5-30ms per sandbox, and E2B uses this technique by default.
E2B cold start is about 150ms with Firecracker microVMs, while Firecracker generally adds 150ms-2s to cold starts.

Firecracker microVMs boot in ~80-200ms with 128-256MB memory per VM and ~5-10% CPU overhead; gVisor boots in milliseconds with 30-50MB per sandbox and ~10-20% CPU overhead; Kata Containers boot in ~500ms-1s.
Firecracker microVMs boot in under 150ms with under 5MB memory overhead, and gVisor adds 5-15% overhead on syscall-heavy workloads but near-zero on typical coding tasks.
gVisor's Sentry reimplements the Linux syscall interface in Go and inspects every syscall before forwarding to the host, costing 10-15% CPU overhead and offering no direct path to GPU hardware.
Firecracker is about 50K lines of Rust versus QEMU's 1.4M lines of C, giving a minimal VMM attack surface; each microVM sandbox has a dedicated kernel.

gVisor's isolation is software-enforced, so a bug in the user-space kernel itself becomes the new escape vector, while standard Docker containers share the host kernel and are insufficient for untrusted code.
E2B has no outbound filtering at all according to this source, and Daytona does not offer network policies by default; egress control is described as missing across much of the market.
In one forum comparison, E2B (Firecracker) had ~150ms cold start with open egress by default, Docker+gVisor runsc had ~380ms, plain Docker with seccomp ~80ms, and Modal containers ~1.5s cold.

Modal uses gVisor by default (VM option available), has no pause state, supports filesystem snapshots with memory snapshots in alpha, and its egress is open by default with block-all, CIDR allowlist, and a beta domain allowlist (443 only).
Modal memory snapshots are experimental and expire after 7 days; its continuous run limit is 5 minutes by default and 24 hours maximum; GPUs are available only with the gVisor runtime.
Modal CPU-bound sandbox cold starts are 2-4 seconds, but its 2025 GPU memory snapshots capture full VRAM state and can push warm-restart latency below 1 second.
Modal's cold start is listed at ~3s in one comparison table, versus Daytona at 90ms, Cloudflare Sandboxes under 50ms, and Blaxel at 25ms resume.
In one comparison Modal Sandboxes (gVisor) are listed at 100-300ms cold start with T4/A10G GPUs and no self-hosting, and Daytona is listed at 200-500ms with Docker+gVisor.

Daytona uses containers by default with VM and Windows classes; egress is restricted on Tiers 1-2 and open on Tiers 3-4, with CIDR (max 10) and domain (max 100) allowlists and block-all; its cold start is claimed under 90ms.

Daytona sandboxes are Linux containers by default, and only VM-class sandboxes support pause, fork, memory snapshots, and nested virtualization; container sandboxes keep filesystem but not memory on stop.
Daytona claims cold starts as low as 27ms using pre-warmed sandbox pools, with Docker/OCI containers by default and optional Kata Containers for VM-level isolation.
Daytona uses a devcontainer.json config standard and achieves sub-90ms container startup via warm pools of pre-built runtimes; its multi-tenant safety is rated Medium versus High for E2B and Modal.

Cloudflare Sandbox is a container in its own VM with 1-3s cold start, open egress by default with options to disable internet or use host allow/deny globs and CIDRs (HTTP/HTTPS only), and only directory backups to R2 for persistence.

Cloudflare Dynamic Workers use V8 isolates that start in a few milliseconds using a few megabytes of memory, claimed 100x faster and 10-100x more memory efficient than containers, with a capability-based model exposing no filesystem, environment variables, or shell.
V8 isolates (Cloudflare Dynamic Workers, open beta April 2026) cannot run arbitrary Linux code, so Python dependencies, filesystem access, or long-running processes are not supported.
E2B and Daytona both charge $0.0504 per vCPU-hour and $0.0162 per GiB-hour (about $0.17 for a busy hour of 2 vCPU/4 GiB), Modal about $0.24, and Cloudflare about $0.22; E2B Pro is $150/month.
